question: to the Commission Assita Kanko (ECR), Malik Azmani (Renew), Aurelijus Veryga (ECR), Jeroen Lenaers (PPE), Lena Düpont (PPE) Subject:

In recent years, EU Member States have tightened their national rules around the acquisition and use of SIM cards. However, in several Member States, identity registration is still not required. Furthermore, even in Member States where it is required, criminals get around it by paying minors to buy SIM cards and then reselling them. This situation constitutes a serious security risk for the EU. SIM cards are used for navigation by operators of drones and smuggling balloons, such as those recently detected over Lithuania. They are also used in disinformation campaigns, and they are used by criminals for scams and phishing operations. In an EU of open internal borders and fee-free roaming, SIM cards obtained in one Member State can be freely used throughout the territory of the EU. With that in mind: 1.
How does the Commission assess the internal security risks of the current situation, whereby several EU Member States do not require identity registration for the purchase of SIM cards?
Does the Commission intend to close this security gap by proposing legislation or by urging the Member States to change their national rules?
Does the Commission agree that, even with registration requirements, more needs to be done to avoid the abusive reselling of SIM cards?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (30.6.2026) The Commission is aware of the growing phenomenon of fraud perpetrated via electronic communications services. Subscriber Identity Module (SIM) cards are the enablers of these services and Member States have the discretion to impose SIM registration requirements, in particular, for pre-paid SIM cards, to counter crimes or any fraudulent activities. These requirements have to comply with EU data protection rules. Obligations on electronic communications service providers to retain subscriber information and other non-content data are currently regulated by national laws. The Commission is currently conducting an impact assessment to evaluate the need for a possible harmonised EU framework on the retention of non-content data for criminal justice purposes. In addition, the proposal for a Digital Networks Act1 requires the Body of European Regulators for Electronic Communications to issue guidelines on measures that could effectively protect end-users against fraudulent activities through interpersonal communications in the EU. National competent authorities will be required to adopt the necessary measures taking the guidelines into utmost account. The Commission will be empowered to adopt delegated acts to supplement the Digital Networks Act with provisions enhancing the effectiveness thereof. Further to the priorities outlined in the ProtectEU Internal Security Strategy2 of April 2025, the Commission intends to publish an Action Plan to counter digital fraud before the end of 2026. As currently envisaged, the Action Plan will aim to address the multifaceted nature of digital fraud through a comprehensive, cross-sectoral approach and specific actions.
